title: The License-Boilerplate Chain
takeaway: Three narrow features from the large A/4 dictionary fire in sequence — on the "A", then on "PARTICULAR", then on "PURPOSE" — with each one raising the probability of the token that triggers the next. Together they reproduce the tail of the standard licence phrase "MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE", which the paper offers as apparent memorization of a string the model saw many times in training.
walkthrough:
You are looking at three [[feature|features]] from a single [[dictionary-learning-run|dictionary learning run]], drawn as a chain of boxes and arrows.

Each grey box is one feature, named in the paper's [[feature-notation|feature notation]]. "A/4/11432" means feature number 11432, found by run 4 of dictionary learning, on the transformer called A. The lines inside a box are [[top-dataset-examples|top activating dataset examples]]: short windows of training text where that feature fired hardest.

To read a box, look for the orange highlight. It marks the one token the feature fired on; the surrounding words are printed only so you can see what that token was sitting in. A darker, bolder highlight means a larger activation.

To read an arrow, read its label. The label is a token whose [[logit-weight]] this feature pushes strongly up — the thing the feature votes for as the next token. The arrowhead points at the feature that fires once that token is actually there.

Now the chain. A/4/11432 fires on the "A" in "…FITNESS FOR A", and predicts " PARTICULAR". A/4/58888 fires on " PARTICULAR", and predicts " PURPOSE". A/4/56745 fires on " PURPOSE", which ends the phrase.

Nothing joins these three in the weights. This is a [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer model]], so each step is a fresh forward pass, and the only channel from one feature to the next is the token that got emitted in between. The paper calls such assemblies [[finite-state-automata-features|finite state automata]] and stresses they are not circuits: the model never learned the parts to cooperate, they line up because the text does.

The paper reads this particular chain as [[memorization-features|sequence memorization]], and notes it shows up only in dictionaries with many features — a small dictionary spends its budget on broad contexts instead, which is [[feature-splitting]].

Then the caveat. This sentence is licence boilerplate sitting in the file headers of popular open-source projects, and the training corpus is [[pile-dataset|the Pile]], so the model saw it many times. Heavy repetition is a plausible reason the chain exists at all — which is the [[model-vs-data-question|model-or-data]] worry in miniature, since a feature this narrow may be tracking a quirk of the corpus more than a computation.

The paper keeps both readings open. It links the chain to a mechanistic account of [[memorization-in-superposition|memorization in superposition]] and to [[mechanistic-anomaly-detection]], calls it surprising that something so specific fits inside 512 neurons at all — an illustration of what [[superposition]] can pack in — and then adds that mechanisms buried this deep in superposition are likely very noisy.

terms.definition: The left-hand feature: number 11432 in dictionary learning run A/4. It fires on the token "A" inside the licence phrase, and its top logit weight is on " PARTICULAR".
The middle feature: number 58888 in the same run. It fires on the token " PARTICULAR" in this phrase, and predicts " PURPOSE".
The right-hand feature: number 56745 in the same run. It fires on " PURPOSE", the last token of the memorized phrase, and closes the chain shown here.
Which transformer the activations came from. A is the main one-layer model the paper studies; B is its seed-twin, used for universality checks and not shown here.
Which dictionary learning run produced the feature. Runs A/0 through A/5 share an L1 coefficient and grow in dictionary size, so A/4 is one of the wide ones.
One learned feature, presented as a card of evidence: its name at the top, and beneath it the dataset snippets on which it activates most.

Marks the token the feature fired on in that snippet. Darker and bolder shading indicates a stronger activation, so the pale highlight on "A" in the left box is a weaker firing than the solid ones in the other two boxes.

A step in the automaton: the source feature raises the probability of the labelled token, and if the model emits it, the target feature fires on the next position. The arrow is a path through the token stream, not a weight connection.
The token A/4/11432 most strongly promotes. The leading space is part of the token, which is how this tokenizer writes a word that begins a new word rather than continuing one.
The token A/4/58888 most strongly promotes, and the token the third feature fires on.
One dataset example inside a box: a window of training text centred on the token where the feature fired, shown in monospace so the tokenization is legible.

terms.term: MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE
terms.definition: The warranty disclaimer this chain reconstructs. It is standard legal wording carried in the file headers of common open-source licences, so it recurs verbatim across large amounts of public code.

Two variants of the same boilerplate visible across the boxes — "MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS" in the left box, "AND FITNESS" in the middle one. Different licence texts word the connective differently, and the features fire across both.
Not a token of interest, just the snippet window cutting off mid-word. It shows the display truncates context rather than the feature responding to a fragment.

The paper's loose name for this shape: features as states, emitted tokens as transitions between them. The label is an analogy, and the paper is careful that the model did not learn the states to work together.

numbers.meaning: The number of features drawn. Three states are enough to carry the phrase from "A" to its end, because each one only has to predict the single next token.
The number of arrows, one fewer than the number of boxes. The last feature's own predictions are not shown here, so the diagram stops rather than closing a loop.
Snippet lines shown per box. It is a display choice, not a count of how often the feature fires; the paper draws its visualizations from a 100-million-token subset of the training data.

Feature indices within run A/4. The numbers themselves carry no meaning or ordering — features come out of the autoencoder unordered — but their five digits indicate a dictionary with tens of thousands of entries.
The run index. The paper says this phrase memorization can be seen only in runs with relatively large numbers of features, which is why the example is drawn from A/4 rather than a small run.

Two things at once. It is the number of neurons in the model's MLP, which is what makes the paper call it surprising that a mechanism this narrow fits inside the model at all; it is also the dictionary size of run A/0, which is why A/0 shows broad context automata and no phrase memorization.

The dictionary sizes of runs A/1 and A/2. The sequence 512 to 4,096 to 16,384 and upward is the axis along which feature splitting happens, with narrower and more specific features appearing as the dictionary widens.

The number of features in A/4 that respond mainly to the token "the" in different contexts. The paper gives it as a sign of how finely a dictionary this wide slices its territory — the same wideness that lets a single phrase get its own chain.
Tokens the one-layer transformer was trained on, deliberately far past compute-optimal. A corpus that large seen for that long is what makes many repetitions of a licence header plausible.
The size of the Pile, the public corpus used for training. Its heavy code content is the reason open-source licence headers are well represented.

The width of the model's residual stream. It is the bottleneck the 512 MLP neurons write back into, and part of why the paper describes these mechanisms as buried deep in superposition and therefore likely noisy.
